content: 1. Assess and treat for signs of heart failure promptly. Refer to page 120 for detailed guidance on management. 2. Administer first aid and arrange immediate transport to the hospital for further care. 3. In cases of severe envenoming, administer scorpion antivenom if available, following the same protocol as for snake antivenom infusion. 4. Treat heart failure if present, as outlined on page 120. 5. Consider the use of prazosin in cases of pulmonary edema, referencing standard pediatric textbooks for dosage and administration. 6. Provide supportive care, including oral paracetamol or oral/intramuscular morphine, based on the severity of pain. 7. For other sources of envenoming, follow the same treatment principles. Administer antivenom if severe local or systemic effects are observed. 8. Venomous spider bites are typically painful but rarely cause systemic envenoming. Antivenom is available for certain species, such as widow and banana spiders. 9. Venomous fish stings can cause severe localized pain, but systemic envenoming is uncommon. Box jellyfish stings, however, can be rapidly life-threatening. 10. Apply vinegar to the sting site using cotton wool to denature the venom proteins. Carefully remove any adherent tentacles without rubbing the area to avoid further venom discharge. 11. Administer antivenom for jellyfish or spider envenoming based on the amount of venom injected. Higher doses may be required for multiple stings, severe symptoms, or delayed presentation. 12. Severe trauma or multiple injuries in children can be life-threatening, affecting multiple organs and limbs. Rapid deterioration may occur due to the cumulative effects of injuries. 13. Management of severe trauma requires urgent recognition of life-threatening injuries and effective teamwork for simultaneous treatment. 14. Conduct a primary survey to identify critical injuries, such as airway obstruction, chest injuries with breathing difficulty, severe hemorrhage, head and cervical spine injuries, or abdominal injuries. 15. Stabilize the neck if there is a risk of neck injury, avoiding unnecessary movement. 16. Expose the child’s entire body to identify injuries, starting with airway assessment, breathing, circulation, and level of consciousness. Control any hemorrhage. 17. Use a systematic approach to assess airway patency, breathing adequacy, circulation, central nervous system function, and cervical spine stability. Document all findings and treatments. 18. Resuscitate the patient as needed, providing oxygen via bag or mask, stopping hemorrhage, and establishing circulatory access for fluid or blood infusion. Draw blood for hemoglobin levels and cross-matching. 19. Conduct a secondary survey only after stabilizing the patient’s airway, breathing, circulation, and consciousness. 20. Perform imaging studies, such as X-rays or ultrasound, based on suspected injuries to diagnose internal hemorrhage or organ damage. 21. Once the child is stable, focus on maintaining homeostasis and arrange transfer to an appropriate ward or referral hospital if necessary. 22. Provide pain relief and reassurance throughout all stages of care. 23. If signs of shock are present, administer 20 mL/kg of normal saline and reassess. If blood is required, give 20 mL/kg of whole blood or 10 mL/kg of packed red cells. 24. Manage hypoglycemia as outlined on page 16. 25. Follow the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) approach for symptom-based diagnosis and treatment, with hospital-level expertise allowing for more precise classifications. 26. Take a detailed history, including personal, vaccination, family, social, and environmental factors, to aid in differential diagnosis and counseling. 27. For young infants, include pregnancy and birth history, as well as feeding history, to identify potential malnutrition or developmental issues. 28. Establish rapport with the child and caregiver before starting the examination. Use a flexible approach to avoid distressing the child unnecessarily. 29. Observe the child’s behavior and physical signs before touching them. Record respiratory rate and other observations before disturbing the child. 30. Perform minimally invasive assessments, such as pulse checks and chest auscultation, before more intrusive procedures like temperature measurement or throat examination. 31. Use pulse oximetry to measure oxygen saturation in children with fast breathing or chest indrawing. 32. Conduct bedside tests, such as blood glucose or rapid malaria diagnostics, when appropriate. 33. Target laboratory investigations based on history and examination findings to narrow the differential diagnosis. 34. Consider microscopy of cerebrospinal fluid, urinalysis, blood grouping, cross-matching, and HIV testing as needed. For neonates, include blood bilirubin levels. 35. Use imaging studies, such as chest X-rays or stool microscopy, to aid in diagnosis. 36. After completing the assessment, compile a list of differential diagnoses to avoid incorrect assumptions and ensure rare conditions are not missed. 37. Plan and initiate treatment based on the main and secondary diagnoses, addressing multiple problems simultaneously if necessary. 38. Review the differential diagnoses after observing the response to treatment or in light of new clinical findings, revising the diagnosis as needed. 39. For newborn care, dry the infant with a clean towel, maintain skin-to-skin contact with the mother, and encourage early breastfeeding to prevent hypoglycemia and hypothermia. 40. Clamp and cut the umbilical cord at least one minute after birth. 41. Neonatal resuscitation may be required for infants born under specific high-risk conditions. Initiate positive pressure ventilation with air for infants over 32 weeks of gestation or with 30% oxygen for very preterm infants. 42. Follow neonatal resuscitation protocols, ensuring adequate chest movement and monitoring heart rate. Adjust ventilation and oxygen concentration as needed. 43. Provide post-resuscitation care and closely observe the infant’s breathing and heart rate.
